patient.name: Carol Ann Whitfield
patient.chiefComplaint: Severe breakthrough abdominal pain, hospice patient with metastatic pancreatic cancer

history.hpi: Patient is enrolled in home hospice for metastatic pancreatic cancer. Daughter and primary caregiver reports the patient's abdominal pain has been escalating over the last two hours, rated 9/10, unrelieved by two doses of her prescribed breakthrough oxycodone. Patient is awake, oriented, and able to communicate her wishes; she states she wants relief from the pain and does not want to go without it out of fear of side effects.
pastMedical: Metastatic pancreatic cancer, enrolled in home hospice
Chronic opioid tolerance from long-term pain management
medications: Extended-release morphine sulfate 60 mg PO twice daily (home regimen)
Oxycodone 10 mg PO PRN breakthrough pain (two doses taken in past hour without relief)
history.lastOralIntake: Sips of water this morning; no solid food due to pain and nausea
history.events: Daughter called the hospice line and then 911 after breakthrough oxycodone failed to control escalating pain

scene.dispatch: 62-year-old female, abdominal pain, hospice patient, residence
scene.location: Single-story home, patient in a hospital bed set up in the living room
scene.safety: No hazards to crew noted; hospice equipment (oxygen concentrator, medication box) present at bedside
scene.bystanders: Daughter present as primary caregiver, gives history and confirms hospice enrollment and home medication regimen
visualCues: Patient grimacing, guarding abdomen, knees drawn up
Hospice comfort kit and medication log visible on nightstand
DNR/POLST form posted on refrigerator per caregiver
Emaciated appearance consistent with advanced malignancy
Home oxygen concentrator present but not currently in use

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 62-year-old hospice patient with metastatic pancreatic cancer, awake and oriented, reporting severe abdominal pain unrelieved by her prescribed breakthrough oxycodone.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, speaking in short sentences due to pain
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, skin warm and dry
otherFindings: No fever, no vomiting at this time
Fully alert and able to converse about her care wishes
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "Please, I need something for this pain, the pills aren't touching it."

expectedActions.shortAction: Assess pain using Numeric Rating Scale (NRS); document 9/10 baseline
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Greater than 12 years old: Self-report scale: Numeric Rating Scale (NRS)
expectedActions.rationale: A documented baseline pain score is required to gauge response to analgesia.

expectedActions.shortAction: Assess abdomen for life-threatening causes (rigidity, rebound, pulsatile mass, distension)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Assess for life-threatening causes of abdominal pain, which may include: Signs and symptoms of ischemic, necrotic, or perforated bowel: Severe tenderness, Abdominal pain with motion or palpation of the abdomen, Fever, Bloody stool
expectedActions.rationale: Even in a known hospice patient, a new surgical abdomen must be excluded before attributing pain solely to the underlying malignancy.

expectedActions.shortAction: Confirm hospice enrollment and consult patient directly on treatment wishes
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Engage with the patient's hospice or end-of-life care team or their primary care physician if possible. If not a viable option, contact medical direction. If the patient can communicate and has the capacity to make decisions regarding treatment and transport, consult directly with the patient before treatment and/or transport
expectedActions.rationale: The patient is alert and has decision-making capacity, so her stated wishes for pain relief should directly guide care.

expectedActions.shortAction: Establish IV access to allow analgesia administration
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Obtain vascular access as necessary to provide analgesia and/or fluid resuscitation
expectedActions.rationale: IV access enables titratable opioid dosing rather than relying on the ineffective oral breakthrough dose.

transitions.condition: Crew obtains a pain scale score, screens the abdomen for life-threatening causes, obtains vascular access, and engages the hospice care framework before administering analgesia.

phases.name: Pain and life-threat assessment performed
phases.description: Crew performs a focused abdominal assessment to rule out a life-threatening surgical cause, scores the patient's pain, obtains IV access, and confirms the patient's hospice status and capacity to direct her own care.
phases.triggerCondition: After the primary survey confirms no immediate airway or breathing compromise, the crew proceeds with a structured pain and abdominal assessment, consistent with treating this as hospice-related breakthrough pain rather than an undifferentiated surgical abdomen.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, 20g IV established left forearm
otherFindings: Pain scale (NRS) 9/10, diffuse abdominal tenderness without rebound or rigidity
No fever, no distension, no pulsatile mass
Confirms hospice enrollment and wants pain relief, no advance directive changes
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I'm hospice, I just want the pain to stop. I know what I want."

expectedActions.shortAction: Hydromorphone 1 mg IV (68 kg × 0.015 mg/kg = 1.02 mg; max initial 2 mg, max cumulative 4 mg)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Hydromorphone: 0.015 mg/kg IM, IV, or IO (maximum initial dose 2 mg; maximum cumulative dose of 4 mg)
expectedActions.rationale: Weight-based initial dosing per protocol, with room to titrate further given her opioid tolerance.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply continuous waveform capnography as early monitor for opioid-induced hypoventilation
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Use of non-invasive capnography is an earlier predictor of hypoventilation than pulse oximetry if opioid medications are administered
expectedActions.rationale: EtCO2 trending detects hypoventilation before SpO2 drops, especially important with additional opioid dosing.

expectedActions.shortAction: Administer full protocol-dosed analgesia; do not withhold for fear of respiratory depression
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Do not withhold opioids for fear of respiratory depression as patient comfort is the primary goal for hospice and end-of-life care
expectedActions.rationale: Hospice goals of care explicitly prioritize comfort over theoretical respiratory depression risk in a patient without current respiratory compromise.

transitions.condition: Crew administers weight-based hydromorphone per protocol, applies capnography, and does not withhold analgesia despite the patient's chronic opioid tolerance.

transitions.if: Opioid withheld over resp depression concern
transitions.condition: Crew delays or withholds hydromorphone out of concern for respiratory depression despite the patient's normal respiratory status and hospice comfort-focused goals of care.

phases.name: Hydromorphone given despite opioid tolerance
phases.description: Crew administers weight-based hydromorphone with continuous capnography monitoring, recognizing that her chronic opioid tolerance and hospice comfort-focused goals of care mean the dose should not be withheld out of fear of respiratory depression.
phases.triggerCondition: After IV access is secured and no life-threatening surgical cause is identified, the crew proceeds with protocol-dosed hydromorphone, applying capnography as the recommended early monitor for opioid-related hypoventilation.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, warm and dry
otherFindings: Capnography waveform normal, EtCO2 within normal limits
No signs of hypoventilation or oversedation
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "That's helping, thank you. Still hurts but it's more bearable."

expectedActions.shortAction: Repeat hydromorphone 1 mg IV after 5 min (cumulative 2 mg; max cumulative 4 mg)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If indicated based on pain assessment, and vital signs allow, repeat pain medication administration (excluding acetaminophen and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicines) after 5 minutes of the previous dose
expectedActions.rationale: Persistent 6/10 pain after the first dose and stable vital signs support a repeat dose within the cumulative maximum.

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess pain score and vitals; transport in position of comfort
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Transport in position of comfort and reassess as indicated
expectedActions.rationale: Ongoing reassessment confirms adequate analgesia without oversedation en route.

transitions.if: Pain reassessed, repeat dose given if needed
transitions.condition: Patient is reassessed at 5 minutes; if pain remains significant, a repeat hydromorphone dose is given per protocol repeat-dosing guidance and the patient is transported in a position of comfort.

phases.name: Pain reassessed, repeat dose given if needed
phases.description: Pain is reassessed five minutes after the initial dose; because it remains only partially controlled, a repeat weight-based hydromorphone dose is given within the protocol's cumulative maximum, and the patient is transported in a position of comfort with her daughter accompanying.
phases.triggerCondition: At the five-minute reassessment interval specified by the Pain Management guideline, persistent pain prompts a repeat dose before transport.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, warm and dry
otherFindings: Pain now 3/10, patient resting more comfortably
No signs of oversedation, appropriately conversant
Positioned semi-fowler's per her comfort preference
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "That's much better. Thank you for listening to me."

phases.name: Opioid withheld over resp depression concern
phases.description: The crew hesitates to give hydromorphone, citing concern for respiratory depression, despite the patient's normal respiratory status, established chronic opioid tolerance, and clearly stated hospice comfort goals. Her pain escalates and she becomes increasingly distressed.
phases.triggerCondition: Crew delays administering analgesia out of a general concern for opioid-related respiratory depression, without regard to the hospice protocol's explicit guidance not to withhold opioids on that basis when comfort is the goal of care.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, skin warm and diaphoretic
otherFindings: Pain unchanged at 9-10/10, patient crying and pleading for relief
Daughter becoming visibly upset at delay in treatment
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "Please, why won't you help me, I told you what I want."

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize hospice guidance: do not withhold opioids for fear of respiratory depression
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Do not withhold opioids for fear of respiratory depression as patient comfort is the primary goal for hospice and end-of-life care
expectedActions.rationale: Continued withholding contradicts the explicit hospice protocol directive and leaves the patient in unrelieved severe pain.
